pr_title: Detect EOF while reading in libssl (1.1.1)
pr_body:
If we hit an EOF while reading in libssl then we will report an error
back to the application (SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL) but errno will be 0. We add
an error to the stack (which means we instead return SSL_ERROR_ssl) and
therefore give a hint as to what went wrong.

WIP because I'd like to check if this actually solves the problem. Also this currently targets 1.1.1 to ease testing by the reporter.

Darn...forgot to add "Fixes #10880"

Ping @openssl/otc. Thoughts?
I'm not on the OTC, but I do agree with the sentiment that this is "just" a bug fix, which would tend to put it on the queue for 1.1.1.

I think the change of behavior is acceptable for 1.1.1. There will be error return anyway, just a different one but with similar handling requirements on the calling application. So no, I do not think this bug fix would be problematic on 1.1.1.

Just as a safety check I'd like a second approval on this PR if possible.

Thanks@beldmit. It seems there is sufficient consensus that this should be backported, so I added the "approval: done" label.

Ref: curl/curl#5138

This may be an issue for us in curl, we allow server truncation by ignoring SYSCALL without an error. Server truncation is very unlikely but continues to be supported for legacy reasons, except in debug builds. Frankly I'd rather we didn't support it at all but we had some reports in the recent past. Regardless it was our intention to eventually treat truncation as an error with later versions of OpenSSL (which I guess would be 3). At this point I think I will suggest we wait for more reports, just to get an idea if this is an issue for curl users that use 1.1.1. 

/cc @bagder

> This may be an issue for us in curl, we allow server truncation by ignoring SYSCALL without an error. Server truncation is very unlikely but continues to be supported for legacy reasons, except in debug builds. Frankly I'd rather we didn't support it at all but we had some reports in the recent past. Regardless it was our intention to eventually treat truncation as an error with later versions of OpenSSL (which I guess would be 3). At this point I think I will suggest we wait for more reports, just to get an idea if this is an issue for curl users that use 1.1.1.

FWIW, in the internal OpenSSL builds I maintain for my employer I chickened out and reverted the associated commits.  In part because I had an unrelated internal issue to address, and did not want to risk having to roll that back if this one bit us.

And my sentiment is roughly in line with yours: would be nice to not have applications unwittingly oblivious of truncation attacks, but risky to spring the mitigation on them in a shared-library update, when by the far the more likely scenario is that the data source is doing sloppy session termination.

This should not affect HTTP though, since HTTP is self-framing with Content-Length, or chunked encoding, but could affect other protocols.  Or am I missing some corner case in HTTP?

> This should not affect HTTP though, since HTTP is self-framing with Content-Length, or chunked encoding, but could affect other protocols. Or am I missing some corner case in HTTP?

Yes legacy servers (or middleboxes maybe), truncation without an HTTP or TLS termination point. We had some reports and had reverted to less sensitivity in curl/curl@78cef06.

> This should not affect HTTP though, since HTTP is self-framing with Content-Length, or chunked encoding, but could affect other protocols.  Or am I missing some corner case in HTTP?

As far as I know, there is a corner case in HTTP 1.1, but not
anymore in 2, but I don't remember the details.

That's correct, it *shouldn't* affect HTTP but it certainly and positively unconditionally will. The world of HTTP(S) is wild and crazy and every imaginable violation of the protocol exists out there. Those violations that we (as a collective) have previously silently accepted will of course especially prevail.

I spent [a significant effort](https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2015/02/12/tightening-firefoxs-http-framing-again/) years ago while employed at Mozilla to try to make Firefox's HTTP code stricter when it comes to this HTTP framing, but eventually had to give up most of the tries simply because there are so many deployed server-side things not adhering and users are not very forgiving when one tool says there's an error with the server while the others don't...

HTTP/2 has much less wiggle room in this department.
Please track issues with this in #11378 rather than here. The current proposal there is to revert this in 1.1.1 but keep it in 3.0. Hearing opinions in that issue would be helpful.

issue_context.title: Data loss with TLS 1.3
issue_context.body:
Hi,

## OpenSSL version:
```
OpenSSL 1.1.1d  10 Sep 2019
built on: Wed Nov 13 16:09:29 2019 UTC
platform: linux-x86_64
options:  bn(64,64) rc4(16x,int) des(int) idea(int) blowfish(ptr)
compiler: gcc -fPIC -pthread -m64 -Wa,--noexecstack -march=x86-64 -mtune=generic -O2 -pipe -fno-plt -Wa,--noexecstack -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -march=x86-64 -mtune=generic -O2 -pipe -fno-plt -Wl,-O1,--sort-common,--as-needed,-z,relro,-z,now -DOPENSSL_USE_NODELETE -DL_ENDIAN -DOPENSSL_PIC -DOPENSSL_CPUID_OBJ -DOPENSSL_IA32_SSE2 -DOPENSSL_BN_ASM_MONT -DOPENSSL_BN_ASM_MONT5 -DOPENSSL_BN_ASM_GF2m -DSHA1_ASM -DSHA256_ASM -DSHA512_ASM -DKECCAK1600_ASM -DRC4_ASM -DMD5_ASM -DVPAES_ASM -DGHASH_ASM -DECP_NISTZ256_ASM -DX25519_ASM -DPOLY1305_ASM -DNDEBUG -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2
OPENSSLDIR: "/etc/ssl"
ENGINESDIR: "/usr/lib/engines-1.1"
Seeding source: os-specific
```

## OS Name, Version, Hardware platform:
Arch Linux, Ubuntu Bionic x86_64

## Compiler Details (name, version):
gcc version 9.2.0

## Problem Description:

When a client sends data to a TLS 1.3 server and then closes the connection, the server won't read everything that was reported as sent on the client side. The amount of data read is non-deterministic.

Reproduction steps:

0. Ignore SIGPIPE
1. TLS client connects to server
2. TLS client sends data (in small chunks, using multiple `SSL_write()` calls)
3. TLS client closes the connection right after returning from all successful (blocking) `SSL_write()` calls
    - Delaying `close()` on the client side with `nanosleep()` or executing a complete TCP shutdown (`shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)`) decreases the possibility of data loss. I guess it's just because this issue has something to do with handling `ECONNRESET` and "new session ticket" messages.

A dummy example can be found here that reproduces the issue (localhost, loopback interface):
https://github.com/MrAnno/openssl-tls13-test/commit/3b101e3441bf69c3e47e73fcea2116718e818119

The data loss usually occurs if the server returns from a blocking `SSL_read()` with `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`:

```
$ ./tls13test
SSL_read returned SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL: Connection reset by peer
read: 3672 (should be 4080)
```

The reason I think it's a bug (even after reading #6904) is because `SSL_read()` sometimes returns with `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`, but the error queue and errno are empty:

```
$ ./tls13test
SSL_read returned SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL: Success
read: 3876 (should be 4080)
```
comments: Can you get a packet trace?  It could be the case that, for example, if the client sends and closes the connection (FIN_WAIT, etc) before the server is done reading *and acknowledging* the data.
This looks like another variation of #7967. TCP's reset semantics do not play well with OpenSSL's TLS 1.3 NewSessionTicket strategy.
Thanks for the reproducer. That's incredibly helpful. Please can you try the patch in #10882 and see if that helps?

@mattcaswell Thank you for the patch.

`SSL_read returned SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL: Success` has now completely disappeared (to be precise, it has been replaced with `SSL_ERROR_SSL - 140676615385664:error:14095126:SSL routines:ssl3_read_n:unexpected eof while reading:ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:302:`), which is great. 

However, I'm still able to reproduce the data loss scenario in case of an `ECONNRESET`.

I'll take a deeper look at my tcpdump as @richsalz suggested.
Have you read #7948?
@kroeckx That must be it! Thank you.

Hi, after the Arch update to OpenSSL 1.1.1e  17 Mar 2020 I'm seeing isync errors like `Socket error: secure read from imap.gmail.com (74.125.133.109:993): error:14095126:SSL routines:ssl3_read_n:unexpected eof while reading` and the exact same thing with the outlook.office365.com IMAP server. It happens after the last mailbox synced in an isync channel. Not sure if connected/helpful, and happy to investigate further if you tell me how.

> Hi, after the Arch update to OpenSSL 1.1.1e 17 Mar 2020 I'm seeing isync errors like Socket error: secure read from imap.gmail.com (74.125.133.109:993): error:14095126:SSL routines:ssl3_read_n:unexpected eof while reading and the exact same thing with the outlook.office365.com IMAP server. It happens after the last mailbox synced in an isync channel. Not sure if connected/helpful, and happy to investigate further if you tell me how.

That comes about because of #10882 which is a fix for one of the problems mentioned in this issue. See:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/c3074077136c698af05ebe57347c186ae15c910a/CHANGES#L22-L27

If you are seeing that message then probably you were already encountering this error prior to updating to 1.1.1e but not getting a useful error message out of libssl and so it was probably not very visible. 1.1.1e gives a more useful error message.

> Hi, after the Arch update to OpenSSL 1.1.1e 17 Mar 2020 I'm seeing isync errors like `Socket error: secure read from imap.gmail.com (74.125.133.109:993): error:14095126:SSL routines:ssl3_read_n:unexpected eof while reading` and the exact same thing with the outlook.office365.com IMAP server. It happens after the last mailbox synced in an isync channel. Not sure if connected/helpful, and happy to investigate further if you tell me how.

Can confirm this, but it seems `mbsync` doesn't lose any data, at least I don't notice any errors.

This happens even if you force `SLLVersions` to TLSv1.2.
Thank you for the quick reply and your work on openssl! Indeed I don't see any signs of data loss either.
The data loss aspect of this issue is entirely separate to the EOF issue - it just so happens that @MrAnno was encountering both. But it is entirely possible to hit one without the other.

I am able to reproduce the issue with https://github.com/MrAnno/openssl-tls13-test/commit/3b101e3441bf69c3e47e73fcea2116718e818119 (without the disabling tickets workaround) with:
- Ubuntu 18.04 with libssl1.1 1.1.1-1ubuntu2.1\~18.04.5, gcc 7.5.0-3ubuntu1\~18.04.
- Arch Linux and openssl 1.1.1.e-1, gcc 9.3.0-1.
- Both are Docker images running on Linux 4.19.76-linuxkit on macOS.

Output (the first "success" output is sometimes repeated even without the workaround):
```
[root@3d92e9d439a1 v]# ./tls13test
read: 4080 (should be 4080)
[root@3d92e9d439a1 v]# ./tls13test
SSL_read returned SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL: Connection reset by peer
read: 408 (should be 4080)
```

Packet captures with embedded secrets: [captures.zip](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/files/4387309/captures.zip)
- ubuntu1804-dsb.pcapng - Ubuntu with 1 success, 1 fail
- archlinux-dsb.pcapng - Arch Linux with 1 success, 3 success (without workaround), 1 fail

In none of the above failing cases a FIN is sent by the client. It seems to be an internal detail regarding handling of NST as mentioned above.
So did you read #7948?

#7948 is concerned about the case where a sending side closes the connection (TCP FIN) while the receiving side sends data over the socket (e.g. NST/close_notify) before reading data. That condition (sending a FIN after client data) does not occur with this reproducer, see the last TCP stream of the capture files above.

With the "fail" case in both captures, we have:
- C->S Finished
- S->C NST
- C->S data (204 bytes)
- S->C NST
- C->S data (204 bytes)
- C->S TCP RST

There is no FIN from the server, the server complains about the client ("SSL_read returned SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL: Connection reset by peer"). The client is at fault for forcifully closing the connection before it transmitted the whole thing.

In the "working" sessions, the client manages to transmit all data in a single TCP segment which may have FIN set. The NST issue from #7948 seems valid, but that is not exactly demonstrated by the reproducer here. Perhaps the server `SSL_get_error` did return an error, but it is not logged. As all bytes were received in the earlier traces before FIN/RST, no complaint occurs. Consider this like a protocol with explicit framing, protecting against truncation attacks as outlined by David in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/7948#issuecomment-562956695.

So to make sure that we both understand what we're talking about:
The client connects to the server, sends data, shuts down the
connection, did not read anything, and closes the connection.

In the mean time the server is trying to send new session tickets
that the client never reads. Depending on the timing sends it
after the client closed the connection.

How is this different from #7948? That you're doing it over
localhost and Linux doesn't send the FIN, just the RST?

It is different from #7948 because the reproducer does not manage to send the full 4080 bytes + close_notify + FIN. Instead it sends 2x 204 bytes, then RST. #7948 seems to require the client to send the FIN before NST is received, that cannot be observed with the current reproducer.

Perhaps the client `SSL_shutdown` in `client_thread` tripped on an error, but its return value is not handled in the reproducer, so it is not clear what went wrong.

Can I suggest you do a strace to see what is going on? As far as I
know, the client did send everything, shutdown, and close the
connection, you just don't see it on the network.
This issue has remained untouched for 4 years, and all the reference PRs are closed.  As such I am closing due to inactivity.  If there is interest in reviving this bug, please feel free to reopen.

I think it would be important to close this ticket with a summary of what happened and steps for mitigating/fixing the problem that was presented originally in #7948, and later here with a different approach.

Back in 2020, I was able to avoid data loss in case of "write-only clients" by setting `SSL_CTX_set_num_tickets(ctx, 0)`:
https://github.com/MrAnno/openssl-tls13-test/commit/61540bc1182065a103f113f2378e9cb5c8758022.

My understanding was that this was a workaround and not a proper resolution of the issue, but I may have misunderstood something.

Please note that the original issue was not theoretical. Applications that implement, for example, FTP and syslog protocols were affected, and they ended up using either the above workaround or something else:


----

<details>
  <summary>Examples of affected projects and their workarounds (click here to expand)</summary>

### proftpd
- https://github.com/proftpd/proftpd/blob/fb6bd090542ee432096df5b136f1b14ec639928e/contrib/mod_tls.c#L7674-L7694

>        * The correct behavior is to wait to send session tickets on the
>        * first call to SSL_write. (This is what BoringSSL does.) So, we
>        * programmatically disable sending/renewing TLSv1.3 session tickets
>        * for the TLS session on data transfers, specifically uploads
>        * (Issue #959).

### syslog-ng and AxoSyslog
- https://github.com/syslog-ng/syslog-ng/pull/3082
- https://github.com/axoflow/axosyslog/commit/28c8013ca35be06387cf692c9ba1baee6af33511

### trio
- https://github.com/python-trio/trio/blob/master/src/trio/_ssl.py#L499-L525

### curl
- claimed to be fixed with https://github.com/curl/curl/issues/6149, but someone still reported problems.
- https://github.com/curl/curl/issues/6149:
  `When I connect using TLS 1.3, I still get a 451 error with select files, but when using --tls-max 1.2 it works fine.`

### poco
- https://github.com/pocoproject/poco/blob/bc29f30e5cf035e860b3d2c1fc5df570f01513ea/NetSSL_OpenSSL/src/SecureSocketImpl.cpp#L107

### duplicati
- unfixed: https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati/issues/4964

### salt
- seems unfixed: https://github.com/saltstack/salt/issues/64550

</details>

----

To avoid any misunderstandings, let me ask the following:

- Is `SSL_CTX_set_num_tickets(ctx, 0)` a workaround?
- What is the correct way of using the OpenSSL APIs with TLS 1.3 if the client only writes application data without reading any (syslog [RFC 5425](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5425), FTP data channel)?
  - Probably the same question rephrased: Have I done something incorrect in the reproducer https://github.com/MrAnno/openssl-tls13-test/commit/3b101e3441bf69c3e47e73fcea2116718e818119 ?
- Among the aforementioned projects, ProFTPD, Trio, and syslog-ng have interpreted that only a workaround can be provided for this issue, which remains part of their codebase to this day. If those do not qualify as workarounds, then it would be important to remove the comments from their code that refer to "unfixed OpenSSL bugs, workarounds" in order to clarify the situation. If they are considered workarounds, then the correct fixes should be implemented for these projects.
-  ProFTPD and Trio have mentioned that BoringSSL handles session tickets differently, which makes this "write-only" use case trivial (this is referred to as "correct behavior" by these projects). What is the OpenSSL stance on this matter?
@nhorman Can you reopen this issue to address these questions/concerns, please?
@mattcaswell can you address the above questions please?

I'll take this question first:

>ProFTPD and Trio have mentioned that BoringSSL handles session tickets differently, which makes this "write-only" use case trivial (this is referred to as "correct behavior" by these projects). What is the OpenSSL stance on this matter?

IIUC, BoringSSL delays sending any session tickets until it first writes any application data. By contrast OpenSSL sends session tickets immediately. This means the BoringSSL approach avoids the problem because it never writes a session ticket in the case where the server never writes any data. I wouldn't say the existing OpenSSL approach is a bug exactly but the BoringSSL approach is definitely better in the "server never writes" scenario.

I think it would be reasonable for OpenSSL to implement an option that would change to this strategy if the option were set. I have raised a feature request for this (#25538).

> - Is SSL_CTX_set_num_tickets(ctx, 0) a workaround?
> - What is the correct way of using the OpenSSL APIs with TLS 1.3 if the client only writes application data without reading any (syslog [RFC 5425](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5425), FTP data channel)?

In the absence of (#25538) this alternative strategy can be implemented "manually" by calling `SSL_CTX_set_num_tickets()` (and if you still want to issue tickets `SSL_new_session_ticket()` - that function delays sending the session ticket until the next write).

It's a bit "clunky" that you have to do it this way for such protocols - but its a perfectly valid and reasonable approach. It seems like the correct approach for now for these protocols. If #25538 gets implemented then probably it would just effectively do it this way "under the hood".

@mattcaswell Thank you for the detailed explanation and for raising #25538.

I think everything is clear now, I'm closing this ticket.

review_comments: Why isn't the "should retry" test enough?

Because if we haven't hit eof  then we want to be returning SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL and have the application check errno to discover the problem. However if we hit eof then errno is not set and do we want to add our own error to the stack (in order to return SSL_ERROR_SSL)
